5. The applicant was born in 1986. Since February 2015 he has been kept in a detention centre for foreign nationals in the town of Makhachkala, Dagestan Republic, Russia.
6. The applicant arrived in Russia in October 2011. He was in possession of a visa declaring the purpose of his visit as business. The applicant’s visa was due to expire in October 2012. However, the visa allowed the applicant to stay in Russia for no longer than ninety days in the course of a single visit. As submitted by the Government, he was therefore expected to leave Russia in early 2012.
7. The applicant did not leave and started to live together with Ms B., a Russian national. In November 2013 they had a child together. In April 2014 they married.
8. In the meantime, on 15 and 19 February 2013 the applicant was found guilty of an offence under Article 18.10 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO), which provided that a foreigner could be punished for unlawful employment activities in Russia.
9. By judgment of 26 February 2015 the Sovetskiy District Court of Makhachkala found the applicant guilty of an offence under Article 18.8 § 1.1 of the CAO (see paragraph 24 below), of remaining in Russia after the expiry of the visa. It sentenced him to a fine and a penalty of forcible administrative removal ( принудительное административное выдворение ) from Russia. The District Court held as follows: “Article 18.8 § 1.1 of the CAO provides for the following penalties: a fine of between 2,000 and 5,000 roubles with or without administrative removal from Russia ... The subsidiary penalty of administrative removal from Russian may be imposed with due regard to the information that confirms the actual need to impose such a penalty on the defendant, as well as the information that confirms the proportionality of this penalty as the only acceptable measure for achieving a balance between the public and private interests at stake ... The defendant has no legal grounds for remaining in Russia. If a fine is imposed, the defendant will add himself to the group of illegal labour immigrants who do everything to avoid compliance with the Russian migration legislation. The penalty of administrative removal is also necessary for the sake of national security, to avoid the spread of various infectious diseases such as HIV, tuberculosis and leprosy, and to ensure the optimal balance of labour resources and in order to support, as a matter of priority, the employment of Russian nationals ...”
10. In the same judgment the District Court ordered that, while awaiting enforcement of the administrative removal, the applicant be placed in a special detention facility for foreigners in the town of Makhachkala.
11. Lawyer D. lodged a statement of appeal on behalf of the applicant against the judgment of 26 February 2015. It appears that the applicant raised arguments relating to his family life in Russia; it is unclear whether he raised any argument relating to a risk to his life and physical integrity in the event of enforcement of the penalty of forcible removal.
12. On 4 March 2015 the Supreme Court of the Dagestan Republic upheld the judgment. The appeal court held as follows: “Article 18.8 § 1.1 of the CAO provides for the following penalties: a fine of between 2,000 and 5,000 roubles with administrative removal from Russia ... [The applicant] has committed a violation of the regime applicable for the presence of foreigners in Russia, by way of omitting after 7 October 2012 to leave Russia ... The court dismisses [the applicant’s] argument relating to his family life in Russia ... The marriage with Ms B. was concluded on 28 April 2014, which was a long time after the commission of the offence by [the applicant] ... The administrative offence record did not contain any information relating to his family life in Russia. No such information was adduced during the proceedings before the first-instance court ... [The applicant’s] prolonged violation of the migration legislation since October 2012 amounts to abuse of Russia’s hospitality and thus should be treated as a breach of the receiving country’s interests ...”
13. On an unspecified date the applicant received a copy of the appeal decision.
14. The penalty of administrative removal was not enforced. According to the Government, the bailiff service instituted enforcement proceedings on 12 March 2015, but they were not pursued on account of an application lodged by the applicant for temporary asylum (see below).
15. On 5 May 2015 the applicant applied for temporary asylum. He referred to the ongoing intensive military actions in Syria, in particular in his home town of Aleppo. He further argued that given his age, he would be drafted by the governmental forces for active military service, thereby putting his life and physical integrity in danger.
16. It appears that the applicant engaged lawyer K. to assist him in those proceedings and had a meeting with him in the detention centre. On 2 June 2015 the applicant called the lawyer from the detention centre, complaining of beatings. On the same day, the lawyer was refused access to the applicant in the detention centre, apparently because he should have obtained authorisation for the visit from the regional migration authority. The lawyer wrote to the regional prosecutor’s office complaining of a violation of the applicant’s rights and physical integrity.
17. On 4 June 2015 the lawyer made a further unsuccessful attempt to gain access to the applicant.
18. On 6 August 2015 the local migration authority dismissed the applicant’s application for temporary asylum. The applicant sought review of this refusal before the Federal Migration Service (“the FMS”). On 24 September 2015 the FMS upheld its decision, stating as follows: “In February 2012 there were no large-scale military operations in Syria; there were only localised hostilities between governmental forces and opposition groups. Despite the above, the applicant failed to leave Russia ... At the time he did not apply for asylum and continued to stay in Russia unlawfully until the imposition of the penalty of administrative removal. The following violations of the migration rules for foreigners should be pointed out: The applicant arrived in Russia under a business visa, whereas his actual goal was employment. Thus, his declared aim did not correspond to the actual aim for arriving in Russia. The applicant was unlawfully engaged in employment activities ... In February 2013 he was twice prosecuted for administrative offences. However, even after this, he did not seek asylum, while neglecting the real possibility of his future deportation from Russia ... The Ministry of Foreign Affairs points out that Syrian nationals who return to their homeland or who are deported or expelled there may arrive in Damascus and then proceed to other regions that are controlled by governmental forces.”
19. On 14 October 2015 the applicant, assisted by lawyer M., sought judicial review of the refusal of temporary asylum under the Code of Administrative Procedure (“the CAP”) and asked the Leninskiy District Court of Makhachkala to put in place an interim measure by way of suspending enforcement of the judgment of 26 February 2015. On 16 October 2015 the court refused to deal with the case, concluding that it had to be lodged before a court with jurisdiction in the area of the applicant’s current “place of residence”; his stay in the detention centre did not qualify as a place of residence.
20. Assisted by Ms Biryukova (who is his representative before this Court) the applicant resubmitted his application for judicial review to the Basmannyy District Court of Moscow. On 27 October 2015 the District Court left the matter without examination because the applicant had not indicated the date and place of his birth; had not specified whether he had a law degree, which was relevant because the case could only be lodged by a person in possession of a law degree; and had not provided evidence that his representative had a law degree. The applicant was required to remedy the above defects by 18 November 2015.
21. By a judgment of 9 December 2015 the District Court upheld the refusals of temporary asylum. The court held that the applicant was at risk of violence which was no more intensive than for other people living in Syria: “The grounds for granting temporary asylum on account of humanitarian considerations include the following situations: a grave medical condition for which the foreigner will not receive the requisite medical care in the country of nationality, thus putting his or her life at risk; a real threat to his or her life or liberty on account of hunger, epidemics, emergency situations of environmental or industrial origin or on account of an internal or international conflict that encompasses the entire territory of the state of nationality; a real threat of being subjected to torture or another cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment in the country of nationality. Under Article 62 of the Code of Administrative Procedure the parties to the case must prove the circumstances to which they refer as the basis for their claims or objections, unless otherwise provided for by the Code. Assessing the evidence submitted to it, the court concludes that [the applicant] has not adduced convincing arguments that he is at risk of being persecuted by the authorities or by groups of the population on account of his religion, race or membership of a social group ... Despite the difficult social and political situation in Syria, there are no grounds to consider that his life will be at a higher risk than that of other people living in this country ... According to information from the Federal Migration Authority, people returning to Syria may reach directly the city of Damascus, which is under the control of the government. ...”
22. The applicant received a copy of the judgment in February 2016 and lodged an appeal. He argued that the first-instance court had not paid proper attention to his argument relating to the risk to his life and physical integrity in the event of his removal to Syria; the migration authority had not refuted his argument while the court had shifted the burden of proof onto the applicant and had placed undue emphasis on the illegality of the applicant’s presence in Russia. His appeal was dismissed by the Moscow City Court on 8 June 2016. The appeal court held as follows: “The first-instance court considered that the applicant did not fall within the scope of the notion of “refugee” under the Refugees Act ... In view of the applicant’s failure to submit specific facts disclosing that in the event of his removal to Syria he would be exposed to a real threat to his security ... or that he was persecuted in this country, the appeal court agrees with the first-instance court ... The appeal court also notes that the applicant arrived in Russia in 2011 but only sought temporary asylum in 2015.”

text_fr:
2. Les requérants sont nés respectivement en 1976 et en 1956 et résident à Makhachkala, au Daghestan. Ils sont représentés devant la Cour par des avocats du Centre des droits de l’homme « Memorial », une organisation non gouvernementale basée à Moscou.
3. Le gouvernement russe (« le Gouvernement ») était représenté par M. M. Galperin, représentant de la Fédération de Russie auprès de la Cour européenne des droits de l’homme.
4. Les faits de l’affaire, tels qu’ils ont été exposés par les requérantes, peuvent être résumés comme suit. Disparition de M. Timur Danilin
5. Les requérantes sont respectivement l’épouse et la mère de M. Timur Danilin, né en 1977. À l’époque des faits, les requérantes et M. Danilin vivaient à Makhachkala, au Daghestan.
6. Le matin du 25 mars 2012, M. Danilin a conduit la première requérante à son travail à bord de sa voiture VAZ-2109. Il était censé venir la chercher à la sortie du travail à 13 heures ce jour-là. Or, il ne s’est pas présenté. La première requérante a tenté de l’appeler, mais en vain.
7. Dans la soirée, la première requérante et ses proches ont commencé à rechercher M. Danilin. Vers 22 heures, la première requérante a reçu un appel provenant d’un numéro inconnu ; c’était M. Danilin, qui lui a dit qu’il avait été roué de coups, que sa voiture et son téléphone portable lui avaient été confisqués et qu’il avait besoin d’aide. Puis un autre homme, qui s’est présenté comme un policier du village de Novolak (également désigné sous le nom de Novolakskoye dans les documents fournis), a demandé à la requérante d’apporter 50 000 roubles (environ 1 300 euros) au poste de police de ce village en échange de la libération de M. Danilin. Lorsque, plus tard dans la soirée, la première requérante, accompagnée d’une douzaine de ses proches, s’est présentée sur place, les agents de police présents au poste ont nié avoir la moindre information sur le lieu où se trouvait M. Danilin et leur ont ordonné de rentrer chez eux, sous peine d’être « eux aussi placés en garde à vue ».
8. Selon les requérants, quelques jours plus tard, des habitants de Novolak leur ont rapporté les faits suivants. Vers 21 h 30, le 25 mars 2012, M. Danilin avait été aperçu, gravement battu, dans une cour de la rue Lenina à Novolak. Il s’était entretenu avec M. L.A., ainsi qu’avec la mère et le frère aîné de ce dernier. C’est alors que l’agent de police de quartier, G.A., qui passait par là, lui a demandé ce qui s’était passé. M. Danilin lui a répondu qu’il avait été roué de coups et qu’on lui avait pris sa voiture et son téléphone.
9. L’agent G.A. a alors appelé la police, qui est arrivée quelques minutes plus tard. L’agent R.Kh. (également désigné sous le nom de R.S. dans les documents fournis) et deux autres agents de police de l’unité d’enquêtes opérationnelles (СОГ) sont sortis du véhicule de police UAZ. Lorsque M. Danilin a aperçu les agents, il a tenté de s’enfuir, mais ceux-ci ont tiré des coups de feu en l’air et l’ont menacé de tirer sur lui. Les agents ont ensuite contraint M. Danilin à monter dans leur véhicule et l’ont emmené au poste de police de Novolak. Peu après, M. Danilin a été transféré du poste de police de Novolak au Centre antiterroriste de Khasavyurt.
10. Le Gouvernement n’a ni contesté les faits exposés par les requérants ni présenté une version alternative des événements. Enquête officielle sur l’enlèvement
11. Le 26 mars 2012, le premier requérant a porté plainte auprès de la police et de la direction du Service fédéral de sécurité (FSB) du Daghestan concernant l’enlèvement de M. Danilin par la police.
12. À l’issue d’un examen préliminaire, le 12 avril 2012, la direction de Khasavyurt du Comité d’enquête a ouvert une procédure pénale en vertu de l’article 105 du Code pénal (meurtre). L’enquête menée dans le cadre de cette affaire pénale peut être résumée comme suit.
13. Le 16 avril 2012, la première requérante s’est vu reconnaître le statut de victime et a été entendue. Dans sa déposition devant les enquêteurs, elle a allégué l’implication de la police dans l’enlèvement de M. Danilin.
14. Le 7 mai 2012, la première requérante a reçu une lettre du service des enquêtes internes du ministère de l’Intérieur du Daghestan, dans laquelle il était indiqué qu’ils « vérifiaient l’implication éventuelle de l’agent de police de quartier G.A. dans la disparition de M. Danilin ».
15. Le 17 mai 2012, le chef du Comité d’enquête du Daghestan a critiqué l’enquête menée dans le cadre de cette affaire pénale, la qualifiant d’inefficace et d’« intentionnellement traînée en longueur », et a ordonné que, « compte tenu de sa médiatisation », elle soit transférée aux enquêteurs du siège du Comité d’enquête du Daghestan.
16. Le 25 mai 2012, le directeur adjoint du Comité d’enquête du Daghestan a critiqué l’enquête, la qualifiant de « menée de manière insuffisamment professionnelle », et a émis des ordres à l’intention des enquêteurs chargés de l’affaire pénale. Ces instructions comprenaient notamment l’obtention des enregistrements des caméras de vidéosurveillance installées le long du périmètre du commissariat de Novolak et l’interrogatoire de tous les policiers qui étaient en service au commissariat de Novolak les 25 et 26 mars 2012.
17. Le 4 juillet 2012, les enquêteurs ont saisi une caméra de vidéosurveillance au poste de police de Novolak afin d’examiner ses enregistrements.
18. Le 5 juillet 2012, les enquêteurs ont interrogé l’agent B.M., qui a déclaré avoir été l’agent de service au poste de police de Novolak le jour de la disparition de M. Danilin. Selon lui, le jour de la disparition, un groupe de quatre ou cinq proches de M. Danilin s’était présenté au commissariat de Novolak. Deux ou trois d’entre eux semblaient ivres et se comportaient de manière agressive. Les proches de M. Danilin n’avaient déposé aucune plainte officielle, mais avaient exigé qu’il leur montre le registre des personnes placées en garde à vue au poste de police, ainsi que les cellules où les détenus étaient retenus. Il avait refusé de le faire. Aucune plainte pour enlèvement n’ayant été déposée, il n’en avait donc enregistré aucune. L’agent B.M. a également déclaré que le commissariat de Novolak disposait de seize caméras de vidéosurveillance et que leurs enregistrements étaient conservés pendant sept jours, après quoi ils étaient écrasés.
19. Deux agents du commissariat de Novolak, R.Kh. et G.A., interrogés par les enquêteurs respectivement les 5 et 9 juillet 2012, ont confirmé qu’ils se trouvaient au commissariat le 25 mars 2012, mais ont nié de manière générale disposer d’informations concernant la disparition de M. Danilin. Ils ont également déclaré que le commissariat disposait de quinze ou seize caméras de vidéosurveillance dans ses locaux et que les enregistrements étaient régulièrement écrasés au bout de quelques jours.
20. Entre le 9 et le 16 juillet 2012, les enquêteurs ont interrogé cinq agents de l’unité des enquêtes opérationnelles du commissariat de Novolak. Aucun d’entre eux ne se souvenait des événements des 25 et 26 mars 2012 en raison du temps écoulé. Ils ont nié disposer d’informations concernant la disparition de M. Danilin et ignoraient pourquoi les proches de M. Danilin pensaient que la police avait été impliquée dans cet incident.
21. Le 16 juillet 2012 (la date indiquée dans les documents fournis était également le 16 juin 2012), les supérieurs hiérarchiques des enquêteurs, relevant de la Commission d’enquête de la Fédération de Russie, ont examiné le dossier d’enquête. À l’issue de cet examen, ils ont critiqué l’enquête, la qualifiant d’inefficace, de trop longue et d’« organisée d’une manière inacceptable ». Ils ont ordonné aux enquêteurs de prendre sans délai un certain nombre de mesures importantes et de leur rendre compte chaque mois des progrès réalisés.
22. Le 7 août 2012, la deuxième requérante s’est vu reconnaître le statut de victime dans l’affaire pénale et a été entendue. Sa déposition rejoignait les allégations des requérants devant la Cour. Selon elle, des agents des forces de l’ordre locales avaient été impliqués dans l’enlèvement puis la disparition de son fils.
23. À plusieurs reprises au cours du mois de septembre 2012, les enquêteurs ont interrogé plusieurs autres agents du commissariat de Novolak, qui ont tous nié disposer d’informations concernant la disparition de M. Danilin.
24. Le 25 octobre 2012, l’expertise de la caméra de vidéosurveillance saisie au commissariat de Novolak a conclu qu’elle ne contenait aucune image et qu’il était impossible de récupérer les enregistrements des 25 et 26 mars 2012.
25. Le 24 décembre 2012, les supérieurs hiérarchiques des enquêteurs ont de nouveau critiqué l’enquête pour ne pas avoir pris les mesures élémentaires, affirmant qu’elle avait été suspendue prématurément et ordonnant la reprise de la procédure.
26. Le 31 janvier 2013, les enquêteurs ont interrogé plusieurs agents du commissariat de Novolak, qui ont tous déclaré ne disposer d’aucune information permettant de savoir si l’un de leurs collègues avait officiellement enregistré des incidents les 25 et 26 mars 2012, y compris celui lié à la disparition de M. Danilin.
27. Le 26 février 2013, les supérieurs hiérarchiques des enquêteurs ont de nouveau critiqué l’enquête pour ne pas avoir pris les mesures élémentaires, affirmant qu’elle avait été suspendue de manière illégale et prématurée et ordonnant la reprise de la procédure. Le document indiquait notamment ce qui suit : « … il ressort de la plainte [déposée par la deuxième requérante contre l’enquête] que la mère de l’agent de police G.A., Mme R., s’était rendue chez [la deuxième requérante] et lui avait dit que, le 25 mars 2012, Timur Danilin avait été roué de coups par des agents de police du commissariat de Novolak et placé dans la cellule de garde à vue de ce commissariat. Il avait réussi à s’échapper et à se réfugier dans la rue [où, dans une cour], il avait rencontré M. L.A., dont il avait utilisé le téléphone pour appeler [la première requérante]… C’est alors que l’agent G.A. est arrivé et… quelques minutes plus tard, une voiture de marque Lada-Priora sans plaque d’immatriculation est également arrivée avec à son bord le chef du commissariat de Novolak, l’agent R. Kh., et deux autres agents, Z.M. et S.A. Les agents avaient tiré plusieurs coups de feu en l’air pour s’assurer que M. Danilin ne s’enfuie pas. Après quoi, les agents avaient fait monter Timur Danilin dans leur voiture et l’avaient emmené au Centre antiterroriste de Khasavyurt. Les habitants des maisons situées à proximité avaient été témoins de l’incident. Le matin du 26 mars 2012, le chef du commissariat de Novolak était revenu sur les lieux et avait averti les riverains de ne rien dire au sujet de l’incident. À ce jour, [le deuxième requérant] n’a pas été interrogé au sujet de cet incident ; de même, Mme R., la mère de l’agent G.A., n’a pas été identifiée ni interrogée… Pour vérifier les informations concernant les personnes détenues au poste de police de Novolak entre le 25 et le 27 mars 2012, il est nécessaire […] d’interroger toutes les personnes qui, selon le registre des détentions du poste, y ont été détenues et qui pourraient donc confirmer si M. Danilin y avait été emmené […] »
28. Le 4 avril 2013, les enquêteurs ont interrogé les requérants au sujet de la plainte déposée par le deuxième requérant auprès de leurs supérieurs. Leurs déclarations ont confirmé les informations fournies dans la plainte (voir le paragraphe ci-dessus).
29. Entre avril 2013 et mars 2014, l’enquête a été suspendue à plusieurs autres reprises et, à chaque fois, elle a été reprise à la suite de critiques formulées par les supérieurs hiérarchiques des enquêteurs, qui ont déclaré que ces suspensions avaient été prématurées et illégales. Le 20 avril 2014, l’enquête a été suspendue pour la dernière fois ; les documents produits montrent que les ordres donnés par les supérieurs n’ont pas été respectés.
30. Il ressort des documents fournis que l’enquête est toujours en cours, que le sort de M. Danilin n’a pas été établi et que les auteurs de son enlèvement n’ont pas été identifiés.
text_de:
2. Die Beschwerdeführer wurden 1976 bzw. 1956 geboren und leben in Machatschkala, Dagestan. Sie werden vor dem Gerichtshof von Rechtsanwälten des Menschenrechtszentrums „Memorial“, einer Nichtregierungsorganisation mit Sitz in Moskau, vertreten.
3. Die russische Regierung („die Regierung“) wurde durch Herrn M. Galperin, den Vertreter der Russischen Föderation vor dem Europäischen Gerichtshof für Menschenrechte, vertreten.
4. Der Sachverhalt des Falles lässt sich, wie von den Beschwerdeführern dargelegt, wie folgt zusammenfassen. Das Verschwinden von Herrn Timur Danilin
5. Die Beschwerdeführerinnen sind die Ehefrau bzw. die Mutter von Herrn Timur Danilin, der 1977 geboren wurde. Zum maßgeblichen Zeitpunkt lebten die Beschwerdeführerinnen und Herr Danilin in Machatschkala, Dagestan.
6. Am Morgen des 25. März 2012 fuhr Herr Danilin die erste Beschwerdeführerin mit seinem Auto, einem VAZ-2109, zur Arbeit. Er sollte sie an diesem Tag um 13 Uhr von der Arbeit abholen. Er erschien jedoch nicht. Die erste Beschwerdeführerin versuchte, ihn anzurufen, jedoch ohne Erfolg.
7. Am Abend begannen die erste Beschwerdeführerin und ihre Angehörigen, nach Herrn Danilin zu suchen. Gegen 22 Uhr erhielt die erste Beschwerdeführerin einen Anruf von einer unbekannten Nummer; es war Herr Danilin, der sagte, er sei geschlagen worden, sein Auto und sein Mobiltelefon seien ihm abgenommen worden und er brauche Hilfe. Dann wies ein anderer Mann, der sich als Polizeibeamter aus dem Dorf Novolak (in den vorgelegten Unterlagen auch als Novolakskoye bezeichnet) vorstellte, die Beschwerdeführerin an, 50.000 Rubel (etwa 1.300 Euro) zur Polizeistation in diesem Dorf zu bringen, um die Freilassung von Herrn Danilin zu erwirken. Als die erste Beschwerdeführerin später am Abend mit etwa einem Dutzend ihrer Verwandten dort eintraf, bestritten die Polizeibeamten auf der Polizeiwache, etwas über den Verbleib von Herrn Danilin zu wissen, und forderten sie auf, nach Hause zurückzukehren, da sie sonst „ebenfalls festgenommen“ würden.
8. Nach Angaben der Beschwerdeführer wurden sie einige Tage später von Einwohnern von Novolak über Folgendes informiert. Am 25. März 2012 gegen 21.30 Uhr sei Herr Danilin schwer geschlagen in einem Innenhof in der Lenina-Straße in Novolak gesehen worden. Er habe sich mit Herrn L.A. sowie dessen Mutter und älterem Bruder unterhalten. Dann habe der zuständige Bezirkspolizist G.A., der zufällig vorbeikam, ihn gefragt, was passiert sei. Herr Danilin habe ihm erzählt, dass er geschlagen worden sei und dass man ihm sein Auto und sein Handy abgenommen habe.
9. Daraufhin habe der Beamte G.A. die Polizei gerufen, die wenige Minuten später eingetroffen sei. Der Beamte R.Kh. (in den vorgelegten Unterlagen auch als R.S. bezeichnet) und zwei weitere Polizeibeamte der operativen Ermittlungseinheit (СОГ) stiegen aus dem UAZ-Polizeifahrzeug aus. Als Herr Danilin die Beamten sah, versuchte er zu fliehen, doch diese gaben Schüsse in die Luft ab und drohten, auf ihn zu schießen. Anschließend hätten die Beamten Herrn Danilin in ihr Fahrzeug gezwungen und seien zur Polizeistation Novolak gefahren. Zu einem späteren Zeitpunkt sei Herr Danilin von der Polizeistation Novolak in das Anti-Terror-Zentrum in Chasawjurt überstellt worden.
10. Die Regierung hat weder die von den Beschwerdeführern vorgebrachten Tatsachen bestritten noch eine alternative Darstellung des Geschehens vorgelegt. Amtliche Ermittlungen zur Entführung
11. Am 26. März 2012 erstattete der erste Beschwerdeführer bei der Polizei und der dagestanischen Dienststelle des Föderalen Sicherheitsdienstes (FSB) Anzeige wegen der Entführung von Herrn Danilin durch die Polizei.
12. Nach einer Voruntersuchung leitete die Abteilung des Untersuchungsausschusses in Chasawjurt am 12. April 2012 ein Strafverfahren gemäß Artikel 105 des Strafgesetzbuchs (Mord) ein. Die Ermittlungen in diesem Strafverfahren lassen sich wie folgt zusammenfassen.
13. Am 16. April 2012 wurde der ersten Beschwerdeführerin der Opferstatus zuerkannt und sie wurde vernommen. In ihrer Aussage gegenüber den Ermittlern behauptete sie, die Polizei sei an der Entführung von Herrn Danilin beteiligt gewesen.
14. Am 7. Mai 2012 erhielt die erste Beschwerdeführerin ein Schreiben der Abteilung für interne Ermittlungen des Innenministeriums von Dagestan, in dem es hieß, man „prüfe die mögliche Verwicklung des Bezirkspolizisten G.A. in das Verschwinden von Herrn Danilin“.
15. Am 17. Mai 2012 kritisierte der Leiter des Ermittlungskomitees von Dagestan die Ermittlungen in dem Strafverfahren als ineffektiv und „absichtlich in die Länge gezogen“ und ordnete an, dass der Fall „angesichts seiner öffentlichen Aufmerksamkeit“ an die Ermittler in der Zentrale des Ermittlungskomitees von Dagestan übertragen werden solle.
16. Am 25. Mai 2012 kritisierte der stellvertretende Leiter des Ermittlungskomitees von Dagestan die Ermittlungen als „unzureichend professionell durchgeführt“ und erteilte den Ermittlern in dem Strafverfahren Anweisungen. Zu diesen Anordnungen gehörten die Beschaffung der Videoaufzeichnungen der entlang des Geländes der Polizeistation Novolak installierten Überwachungskameras sowie die Vernehmung aller Polizeibeamten, die am 25. und 26. März 2012 in der Polizeistation Novolak Dienst hatten.
17. Am 4. Juli 2012 beschlagnahmten die Ermittler eine Überwachungskamera aus der Polizeistation Novolak, um deren Aufzeichnungen zu untersuchen.
18. Am 5. Juli 2012 befragten die Ermittler den Beamten B.M., der angab, am Tag des Verschwindens von Herrn Danilin der diensthabende Beamte auf der Polizeiwache in Novolak gewesen zu sein. Seinen Angaben zufolge sei am Tag des Verschwindens eine Gruppe von vier oder fünf Angehörigen von Herrn Danilin auf der Polizeiwache in Novolak eingetroffen. Zwei oder drei von ihnen hätten betrunken gewirkt und sich aggressiv verhalten. Die Angehörigen von Herrn Danilin hätten keine offiziellen Anzeigen erstattet, sondern verlangt, dass er ihnen das Verzeichnis der auf der Polizeiwache festgehaltenen Personen sowie die Zellen zeige, in denen die Festgenommenen untergebracht waren. Er habe sich geweigert, dies zu tun. Da keine Anzeigen wegen Entführung erstattet worden waren, habe er auch keine registriert. Beamter B.M. gab ferner an, dass die Polizeiwache Novolak über sechzehn Überwachungskameras verfüge und deren Aufzeichnungen sieben Tage lang gespeichert würden, bevor sie überschrieben würden.
19. Zwei Polizeibeamte der Polizeistation Novolak, R.Kh. und G.A., die am 5. bzw. 9. Juli 2012 von den Ermittlern befragt wurden, bestätigten, dass sie sich am 25. März 2012 auf der Polizeistation aufgehalten hatten, bestritten jedoch allgemein, über Informationen zum Verschwinden von Herrn Danilin zu verfügen. Sie gaben außerdem an, dass die Polizeiwache auf ihrem Gelände entweder fünfzehn oder sechzehn Überwachungskameras besaß und dass das Bildmaterial regelmäßig nach einigen Tagen überschrieben wurde.
20. Zwischen dem 9. und 16. Juli 2012 befragten die Ermittler fünf Beamte der operativen Ermittlungsabteilung der Polizeiwache Novolak. Keiner von ihnen konnte sich aufgrund des Zeitablaufs an die Ereignisse vom 25. und 26. März 2012 erinnern. Sie bestritten, über Informationen zum Verschwinden von Herrn Danilin zu verfügen, und hatten keine Ahnung, warum die Angehörigen von Herrn Danilin der Meinung sein könnten, die Polizei sei in den Vorfall verwickelt gewesen.
21. Am 16. Juli 2012 (in den vorgelegten Unterlagen wurde als Datum auch der 16. Juni 2012 angegeben) prüften die Vorgesetzten der Ermittler vom Untersuchungsausschuss der Russischen Föderation die Ermittlungsakte. Infolgedessen kritisierten sie die Ermittlungen als ineffektiv, langwierig und „in unzumutbar schlechter Weise organisiert“. Sie wiesen die Ermittler an, unverzüglich eine Reihe wichtiger Maßnahmen zu ergreifen und ihnen monatlich über die erzielten Fortschritte Bericht zu erstatten.
22. Am 7. August 2012 wurde der zweiten Beschwerdeführerin in dem Strafverfahren der Opferstatus zuerkannt und sie wurde vernommen. Ihre Aussage entsprach den vor dem Gerichtshof vorgebrachten Ausführungen der Beschwerdeführer. Ihrer Ansicht nach waren Beamte der örtlichen Strafverfolgungsbehörden an der Entführung und dem anschließenden Verschwinden ihres Sohnes beteiligt gewesen.
23. An verschiedenen Tagen im September 2012 befragten die Ermittler mehrere weitere Beamte der Polizeidienststelle Novolak, die alle bestritten, über Informationen zum Verschwinden von Herrn Danilin zu verfügen.
24. Am 25. Oktober 2012 kam die Begutachtung der aus der Polizeistation Novolak beschlagnahmten Überwachungskamera zu dem Ergebnis, dass diese keine Aufzeichnungen enthielt und es unmöglich war, die Aufnahmen vom 25. und 26. März 2012 wiederherzustellen.
25. Am 24. Dezember 2012 kritisierten die Vorgesetzten der Ermittler erneut, dass bei den Ermittlungen grundlegende Schritte versäumt worden seien, erklärten, dass diese vorzeitig eingestellt worden seien, und ordneten die Wiederaufnahme des Verfahrens an.
26. Am 31. Januar 2013 befragten die Ermittler mehrere Beamte der Polizeistation Novolak, die alle angaben, keine Informationen darüber zu haben, ob einer ihrer Kollegen am 25. und 26. März 2012 Vorfälle offiziell registriert hatte, einschließlich des Vorfalls im Zusammenhang mit dem Verschwinden von Herrn Danilin.
27. Am 26. Februar 2013 kritisierten die Vorgesetzten der Ermittler erneut, dass bei den Ermittlungen grundlegende Schritte versäumt worden seien; sie stellten fest, dass diese rechtswidrig und vorzeitig ausgesetzt worden seien, und ordneten die Wiederaufnahme des Verfahrens an. In dem Dokument hieß es insbesondere: „… aus der Beschwerde [die die zweite Beschwerdeführerin gegen die Ermittlungen eingereicht hatte] geht hervor, dass die Mutter des Polizeibeamten G.A., Frau R., [die zweite Beschwerdeführerin] zu Hause aufgesucht und ihr erzählt habe, dass Timur Danilin am 25. März 2012 von Polizeibeamten der Polizeistation Novolak geschlagen und in die vorübergehende Haftzelle der Station gebracht worden sei. Es sei ihm gelungen, zu fliehen und auf die Straße zu laufen [wo er in einem Innenhof] Herrn L.A. begegnet sei, dessen Telefon er benutzt habe, um [die erste Beschwerdeführerin] anzurufen … Dann sei der Polizeibeamte G.A. eingetroffen und … einige Minuten später sei auch ein Lada-Priora-Pkw ohne Kennzeichen mit dem Leiter der Polizeistation Novolak, dem Polizeibeamten R. Kh., und zwei weiteren Polizeibeamten, Z.M. und S.A. Die Beamten hatten mehrere Schüsse in die Luft abgegeben, um sicherzustellen, dass Herr Danilin nicht fliehen würde. Danach hatten die Beamten Timur Danilin in ihr Fahrzeug gesetzt und ihn zum Anti-Terror-Zentrum in Chasawjurt gebracht. Die Bewohner der in der Nähe gelegenen Häuser hatten den Vorfall beobachtet. Am Morgen des 26. März 2012 war der Leiter der Polizeistation Novolak zum Tatort zurückgekehrt und hatte die Anwohner gewarnt, über den Vorfall zu schweigen. Bis heute wurde [der zweite Beschwerdeführer] nicht zu diesem Vorfall befragt; ebenso wenig wurde Frau R., die Mutter des Beamten G.A., identifiziert und befragt … Um die Angaben zu den Personen zu überprüfen, die zwischen dem 25. und 27. März 2012 auf der Polizeiwache Novolak festgehalten wurden, ist es erforderlich …, alle Personen zu befragen, die laut dem Festhaltprotokoll der Wache dort festgehalten wurden und daher bestätigen könnten, ob Herr Danilin dorthin gebracht worden war …“
28. Am 4. April 2013 befragten die Ermittler die Beschwerdeführer zu der Beschwerde, die der zweite Beschwerdeführer bei den Vorgesetzten der Ermittler eingereicht hatte. Ihre Aussagen bestätigten die in der Beschwerde gemachten Angaben (siehe den vorstehenden Absatz).
29. Zwischen April 2013 und März 2014 wurde die Ermittlung noch mehrmals ausgesetzt und jedes Mal aufgrund von Kritik seitens der Vorgesetzten der Ermittler wieder aufgenommen, die erklärten, die Aussetzungen seien voreilig und rechtswidrig gewesen. Am 20. April 2014 wurde die Ermittlung ein letztes Mal ausgesetzt; aus den vorgelegten Unterlagen geht hervor, dass die Anordnungen der Vorgesetzten nicht befolgt wurden.
30. Aus den vorgelegten Unterlagen geht hervor, dass die Ermittlungen noch andauern, der Verbleib von Herrn Danilin nicht geklärt ist und die Täter seiner Entführung nicht identifiziert wurden.
text_it:
2. I ricorrenti sono nati rispettivamente nel 1976 e nel 1956 e risiedono a Makhachkala, nel Daghestan. Sono rappresentati dinanzi alla Corte dagli avvocati del Centro per i diritti umani “Memorial”, un’organizzazione non governativa con sede a Mosca.
3. Il Governo russo («il Governo») era rappresentato dal sig. M. Galperin, rappresentante della Federazione Russa presso la Corte europea dei diritti dell’uomo.
4. I fatti del caso, così come esposti dai ricorrenti, possono essere sintetizzati come segue. Scomparsa del sig. Timur Danilin
5. Le ricorrenti sono rispettivamente la moglie e la madre del sig. Timur Danilin, nato nel 1977. All’epoca dei fatti, le ricorrenti e il sig. Danilin vivevano a Makhachkala, nel Daghestan.
6. La mattina del 25 marzo 2012 il sig. Danilin ha accompagnato la prima ricorrente al lavoro con la sua auto VAZ-2109. Avrebbe dovuto passare a prenderla al lavoro alle 13:00 di quel giorno. Tuttavia, non si è presentato. La prima ricorrente ha provato a chiamarlo, ma senza successo.
7. In serata, la prima ricorrente e i suoi familiari hanno iniziato a cercare il signor Danilin. Verso le ore 22:00 la prima ricorrente ha ricevuto una chiamata da un numero sconosciuto; era il signor Danilin, il quale ha riferito di essere stato picchiato, di essersi fatto sottrarre l’auto e il cellulare e di aver bisogno di aiuto. Successivamente, un altro uomo che si è presentato come agente di polizia del villaggio di Novolak (indicato anche come Novolakskoye nei documenti presentati) ha detto alla ricorrente di portare 50.000 rubli (circa 1.300 euro) alla stazione di polizia di quel villaggio in cambio del rilascio del signor Danilin. Quando, più tardi quella sera, la prima ricorrente, accompagnata da una dozzina di suoi parenti, giunse sul posto, gli agenti di polizia presenti alla stazione negarono di essere a conoscenza del luogo in cui si trovava il signor Danilin e intimarono loro di tornare a casa, pena il «fermo anche per loro».
8. Secondo i ricorrenti, alcuni giorni dopo sono stati informati dagli abitanti di Novolak di quanto segue. Verso le 21.30 del 25 marzo 2012 il signor Danilin era stato visto, gravemente picchiato, in un cortile in via Lenina a Novolak. Stava parlando con il signor L.A., con la madre e con il fratello maggiore di quest’ultimo. A quel punto l’agente di quartiere G.A., che stava passando di lì, gli aveva chiesto cosa fosse successo. Il signor Danilin gli aveva detto di essere stato picchiato e che gli erano stati sottratti l’auto e il telefono.
9. L’agente G.A. aveva quindi chiamato la polizia, che era arrivata pochi minuti dopo. L’agente R.Kh. (indicato anche come R.S. nei documenti presentati) e altri due agenti dell’unità investigativa operativa (СОГ) erano scesi dal veicolo UAZ della polizia. Quando il signor Danilin aveva visto gli agenti, aveva cercato di scappare, ma questi avevano sparato colpi in aria e minacciato di sparargli. Successivamente gli agenti hanno costretto il sig. Danilin a salire sul loro veicolo e lo hanno portato alla stazione di polizia di Novolak. In un momento successivo il sig. Danilin è stato trasferito dalla stazione di polizia di Novolak al Centro antiterrorismo di Khasavyurt.
10. Il Governo non ha contestato i fatti esposti dai ricorrenti né ha avanzato una versione alternativa degli eventi. Indagine ufficiale sul rapimento
11. Il 26 marzo 2012 il primo ricorrente ha sporto denuncia alla polizia e al Dipartimento del Dagestan del Servizio Federale di Sicurezza (FSB) in merito al rapimento del signor Danilin da parte della polizia.
12. A seguito di un esame preliminare, il 12 aprile 2012 il Dipartimento di Khasavyurt del Comitato Investigativo ha avviato un procedimento penale ai sensi dell’articolo 105 del Codice penale (omicidio). L’andamento delle indagini nel procedimento penale può essere sintetizzato come segue.
13. Il 16 aprile 2012 alla prima ricorrente è stato riconosciuto lo status di vittima ed è stata interrogata. Nella sua dichiarazione agli investigatori, ha denunciato il coinvolgimento della polizia nel rapimento del sig. Danilin.
14. Il 7 maggio 2012 la prima ricorrente ha ricevuto una lettera dal Dipartimento delle indagini interne del Ministero dell’Interno del Daghestan in cui si affermava che stavano «verificando il potenziale coinvolgimento dell’agente di polizia di quartiere G.A. nella scomparsa del sig. Danilin».
15. Il 17 maggio 2012 il capo del Comitato Investigativo del Daghestan ha criticato l’indagine sul procedimento penale definendola inefficace e «volutamente protratta» e ha ordinato che, «vista la sua risonanza mediatica», fosse trasferita agli investigatori presso la sede centrale del Comitato Investigativo del Daghestan.
16. Il 25 maggio 2012 il vice capo del Comitato Investigativo del Daghestan ha criticato l’indagine definendola «condotta in modo insufficientemente professionale» e ha emanato una serie di ordini che gli investigatori incaricati del caso penale dovevano eseguire. Tali ordini includevano l’acquisizione delle riprese delle telecamere a circuito chiuso installate lungo il perimetro della stazione di polizia di Novolak e l’interrogatorio di tutti gli agenti di polizia che erano in servizio presso la stazione di polizia di Novolak il 25 e il 26 marzo 2012.
17. Il 4 luglio 2012 gli investigatori hanno sequestrato una telecamera a circuito chiuso dalla stazione di polizia di Novolak per esaminarne le riprese.
18. Il 5 luglio 2012 gli investigatori hanno interrogato l’agente B.M., il quale ha dichiarato di essere stato l’agente in servizio presso la stazione di polizia di Novolak alla data della scomparsa del sig. Danilin. Secondo lui, il giorno della scomparsa, un gruppo di quattro o cinque parenti del signor Danilin si era presentato alla stazione di polizia di Novolak. Due o tre di loro sembravano ubriachi e si comportavano in modo aggressivo. I parenti del signor Danilin non avevano presentato alcuna denuncia ufficiale, ma avevano preteso che lui mostrasse loro il registro delle persone trattenute presso la stazione di polizia, nonché le celle in cui erano rinchiusi i detenuti. Lui si era rifiutato di farlo. Poiché non era stata presentata alcuna denuncia di rapimento, non ne aveva registrata alcuna. L’agente B.M. ha inoltre dichiarato che la stazione di polizia di Novolak disponeva di sedici telecamere a circuito chiuso e che le registrazioni venivano conservate per sette giorni, dopodiché venivano sovrascritte.
19. Due agenti della stazione di polizia di Novolak, R.Kh. e G.A., interrogati dagli investigatori rispettivamente il 5 e il 9 luglio 2012, hanno confermato di trovarsi alla stazione di polizia il 25 marzo 2012, ma hanno negato in termini generali di possedere informazioni relative alla scomparsa del sig. Danilin. Hanno inoltre dichiarato che la stazione di polizia disponeva di quindici o sedici telecamere a circuito chiuso nei propri locali e che le registrazioni venivano regolarmente sovrascritte dopo alcuni giorni.
20. Tra il 9 e il 16 luglio 2012 gli investigatori hanno interrogato cinque agenti dell’unità investigativa operativa della stazione di polizia di Novolak. Nessuno di loro riusciva a ricordare gli eventi del 25 e 26 marzo 2012 a causa del tempo trascorso. Hanno negato di possedere informazioni relative alla scomparsa del signor Danilin e non avevano idea del motivo per cui i parenti del signor Danilin potessero ritenere che la polizia fosse stata coinvolta nell’incidente.
21. Il 16 luglio 2012 (data indicata anche come 16 giugno 2012 nei documenti presentati), i superiori degli investigatori, appartenenti al Comitato Investigativo della Federazione Russa, hanno esaminato il fascicolo dell’indagine. Di conseguenza, hanno criticato l’indagine definendola inefficace, protratta nel tempo e «organizzata in modo inaccettabilmente carente». Hanno ordinato agli investigatori di adottare senza indugio una serie di misure importanti e di riferire loro mensilmente sui progressi compiuti.
22. Il 7 agosto 2012 alla seconda ricorrente è stato riconosciuto lo status di parte lesa nel procedimento penale ed è stata interrogata. La sua dichiarazione era simile a quanto esposto dai ricorrenti dinanzi alla Corte. A suo avviso, agenti delle forze dell’ordine locali erano stati coinvolti nel rapimento e nella successiva scomparsa di suo figlio.
23. In diverse date del settembre 2012 gli investigatori hanno interrogato diversi altri agenti della stazione di polizia di Novolak, i quali hanno tutti negato di disporre di informazioni relative alla scomparsa del sig. Danilin.
24. Il 25 ottobre 2012 la perizia sulla telecamera a circuito chiuso sequestrata presso la stazione di polizia di Novolak ha concluso che essa non conteneva alcuna registrazione e che era impossibile recuperare le riprese del 25 e 26 marzo 2012.
25. Il 24 dicembre 2012 i superiori degli investigatori hanno nuovamente criticato l’indagine per non aver adottato le misure di base, affermando che era stata sospesa prematuramente e ordinando la ripresa del procedimento.
26. Il 31 gennaio 2013 gli investigatori hanno interrogato diversi agenti della stazione di polizia di Novolak, i quali hanno tutti dichiarato di non avere informazioni sul fatto che qualcuno dei loro colleghi avesse registrato ufficialmente eventuali incidenti avvenuti il 25 e il 26 marzo 2012, compreso quello relativo alla scomparsa del signor Danilin.
27. Il 26 febbraio 2013 i superiori degli investigatori hanno nuovamente criticato l’indagine per non aver adottato le misure di base, affermando che era stata sospesa in modo illegittimo e prematuro e ordinando la ripresa del procedimento. Il documento riportava, in particolare, quanto segue: «... dalla denuncia [presentata dalla seconda ricorrente contro l’indagine] emerge che la madre dell’agente di polizia G.A., la signora R., si fosse recata a casa [della seconda ricorrente] e le avesse riferito che il 25 marzo 2012 Timur Danilin era stato picchiato da agenti di polizia della stazione di Novolak e rinchiuso nel centro di detenzione temporanea della stazione. Era riuscito a fuggire e a correre in strada [dove, in un cortile,] aveva incontrato il signor L.A., di cui aveva usato il telefono per chiamare [la prima ricorrente] ... A quel punto era arrivato l’agente G.A. e… alcuni minuti dopo era giunta anche un’auto Lada-Priora senza targa con a bordo il capo della stazione di polizia di Novolak, l’agente R. Kh., e altri due agenti, Z.M. e S.A. Gli agenti avevano sparato diversi colpi in aria per assicurarsi che il signor Danilin non fuggisse. Successivamente gli agenti avevano fatto salire Timur Danilin sulla loro auto e lo avevano condotto al Centro antiterrorismo di Khasavyurt. I residenti delle abitazioni situate nelle vicinanze avevano assistito all’incidente. La mattina del 26 marzo 2012 il capo della stazione di polizia di Novolak era tornato sul posto e aveva intimato ai residenti locali di tacere sull’accaduto. Ad oggi, [il secondo ricorrente] non è stato interrogato in merito a questo episodio; né la signora R., madre dell’agente G.A., è stata identificata e interrogata ... Per verificare le informazioni relative alle persone detenute presso la stazione di polizia di Novolak tra il 25 e il 27 marzo 2012, è necessario ... interrogare tutte le persone che, secondo il registro delle detenzioni della stazione, vi erano state trattenute e che potrebbero quindi confermare se il sig. Danilin vi fosse stato condotto ...”
28. Il 4 aprile 2013 gli investigatori hanno interrogato i ricorrenti in merito alla denuncia presentata dal secondo ricorrente ai superiori degli investigatori. Le loro dichiarazioni hanno confermato le informazioni fornite nella denuncia (cfr. il paragrafo precedente).
29. Tra aprile 2013 e marzo 2014 l’indagine è stata sospesa in diverse altre occasioni e ogni volta è stata ripresa a seguito delle critiche mosse dai superiori degli investigatori, i quali hanno affermato che le sospensioni erano state premature e illegali. Il 20 aprile 2014 l’indagine è stata sospesa per l’ultima volta; dai documenti presentati risulta che gli ordini impartiti dai superiori non sono stati rispettati.
30. Dai documenti presentati risulta che l’indagine è ancora in corso, che non è stato accertato dove si trovi il sig. Danilin e che gli autori del suo rapimento non sono stati identificati.

2. The applicants were born in 1976 and 1956 respectively and live in Makhachkala, Dagestan. They are represented before the Court by lawyers from Memorial Human Rights Centre, a non-governmental organisation in Moscow.
3. The Russian Government (“the Government”) were represented by Mr M. Galperin, the Representative of the Russian Federation to the European Court of Human Rights.
4. The facts of the case, as submitted by the applicants, may be summarised as follows. Disappearance of M r Timur Danilin
5. The applicants are the wife and mother respectively of Mr Timur Danilin, who was born in 1977. At the material time, the applicants and Mr Danilin lived in Makhachkala, Dagestan.
6. On the morning of 25 March 2012 Mr Danilin took the first applicant to work in his VAZ-2109 car. He was supposed to pick her up from work at 1 p.m. that day. However, he did not arrive. The first applicant tried calling him, but to no avail.
7. In the evening, the first applicant and her relatives started searching for Mr Danilin. At about 10 p.m. the first applicant received a call from an unfamiliar number; it was Mr Danilin, who said that he had been beaten, his car and mobile phone had been taken from him and he needed help. Then another man who introduced himself as a police officer from the village of Novolak (also referred to as Novolakskoye in the documents submitted) told the applicant to bring 50,000 roubles (about 1,300 euros) to the police station in that village in exchange for Mr Danilin’s release. When later in the evening the first applicant with about a dozen of her relatives arrived there, the police officers at the police station denied any knowledge of Mr Danilin’s whereabouts and demanded that they return home or they would be “detained as well”.
8. According to the applicants, several days later they were informed by the residents of Novolak of the following. At about 9.30 p.m. on 25 March 2012 Mr Danilin had been seen, severely beaten, in a courtyard in Lenina Street in Novolak. He had been speaking with Mr L.A. and the latter’s mother and elder brother. Then the neighbourhood police officer, G.A., who had been passing by, asked him what had happened. Mr Danilin had told him that he had been beaten, and that his car and his phone had been taken from him.
9. Then Officer G.A. had called the police, who had arrived a few minutes later. Officer R.Kh. (also referred to as R.S. in the documents submitted) and two other police officers from the operational investigations unit (СОГ) had emerged from the police UAZ vehicle. When Mr Danilin had seen the officers, he had tried to run away, but they had fired shots in the air and threatened to shoot him. Then the officers had forced Mr Danilin into their vehicle and driven off to the Novolak police station. At some point later Mr Danilin had been transferred from the Novolak police station to the Khasavyurt Counterterrorism Centre.
10. The Government neither contested the facts as submitted by the applicants nor advanced an alternative version of the events. Official investigation into the abduction
11. On 26 March 2012 the first applicant complained to the police and the Dagestan Department of the Federal Security Service (FSB) of Mr Danilin’s abduction by the police.
12. Following a preliminary examination, on 12 April 2012 the Khasavyurt Department of the Investigative Committee opened a criminal case under Article 105 of the Criminal Code (murder). The investigation of the criminal case can be summarised as follows.
13. On 16 April 2012 the first applicant was granted victim status and questioned. In her statement to the investigators, she alleged the involvement of the police in the abduction of Mr Danilin.
14. On 7 May 2012 the first applicant received a letter from the Internal Investigations Department of the Dagestan Ministry of the Interior which stated that they “were verifying the potential involvement of the neighbourhood police officer G.A. in the disappearance of Mr Danilin”.
15. On 17 May 2012 the head of the Dagestan Investigative Committee criticised the investigation of the criminal case as ineffective and “intentionally dragged out” and ordered that “in view of its publicity” it be transferred to the investigators at the headquarters of the Dagestan Investigative Committee.
16. On 25 May 2012 the deputy head of the Dagestan Investigative Committee criticised the investigation as “carried out in an insufficiently professional manner” and issued orders to be carried out by the investigators in the criminal case. Those orders included obtaining the CCTV footage from the cameras installed along the perimeter of the Novolak police station and questioning of all of the police officers who were on duty at the Novolak police station on 25 and 26 March 2012.
17. On 4 July 2012 the investigators seized one CCTV camera from the Novolak police station to examine its footage.
18. On 5 July 2012 the investigators questioned Officer B.M., who stated that he had been the on-duty officer at the Novolak police station on the date of Mr Danilin’s disappearance. According to him, on the date of the disappearance, a group of four or five of Mr Danilin’s relatives had arrived at the Novolak police station. Two or three of them had seemed drunk and behaved aggressively. Mr Danilin’s relatives had not lodged any official complaints, but had demanded that he show them the log of the persons detained at the police station, as well as the cells where the detainees were kept. He had refused to do so. Given that no complaints of abduction had been lodged, he had not registered any. Officer B.M. also stated that the Novolak police station had sixteen CCTV cameras and their footage was stored for seven days, after which it was overwritten.
19. Two police officers from the Novolak police station, R.Kh. and G.A., questioned by the investigators on 5 and 9 July 2012 respectively, confirmed that they had been at the police station on 25 March 2012, but denied in general terms having any information pertaining to the disappearance of Mr Danilin. They also stated that the police station had either fifteen or sixteen CCTV cameras on its premises and that the footage was regularly overwritten after several days.
20. Between 9 and 16 July 2012 the investigators questioned five officers from the Novolak police station’s operational investigations unit. None of them could recall the events of 25 and 26 March 2012 owing to the passage of time. They denied having any information concerning the disappearance of Mr Danilin and had no idea why Mr Danilin’s relatives would think that the police had been involved in the incident.
21. On 16 July 2012 (the date was also given as 16 June 2012 in the documents submitted), the investigators’ superiors from the Investigative Committee of the Russian Federation reviewed the investigation file. As a result, they criticised the investigation as ineffective, protracted and “organised in an unacceptably poor manner”. They ordered that the investigators take a number of important steps without delay and report to them on a monthly basis on the progress made.
22. On 7 August 2012 the second applicant was granted victim status in the criminal case and questioned. Her statement was similar to the applicants’ submissions before the Court. In her opinion, officers from local law-enforcement agencies had been involved in the abduction and subsequent disappearance of her son.
23. On various dates in September 2012 the investigators questioned several more officers from the Novolak police station, all of whom denied having any information concerning Mr Danilin’s disappearance.
24. On 25 October 2012 the expert examination of the CCTV camera seized from the Novolak police station concluded that it did not contain any footage and that it was impossible to recover the footage from 25 and 26 March 2012.
25. On 24 December 2012 the investigators’ superiors again criticised the investigation for failing to take basic steps, stating that it had been suspended prematurely and ordering that the proceedings be resumed.
26. On 31 January 2013 the investigators questioned several officers from the Novolak police station, all of whom stated that they had no information as to whether any of their colleagues had officially registered any incidents on 25 and 26 March 2012, including the one relating to Mr Danilin’s disappearance.
27. On 26 February 2013 the investigators’ superiors again criticised the investigation for failing to take basic steps, stating that it had been suspended unlawfully and prematurely and ordering that the proceedings be resumed. The document stated, in particular, the following: “... it transpires from the complaint [that the second applicant lodged against the investigation] that the mother of police officer G.A., Ms R., had visited [the second applicant] at home and told her that on 25 March 2012 Timur Danilin had been beaten by police officers from the Novolak police station and placed in the temporary detention unit at the station. He had managed to escape and run into the street [where, in a courtyard,] he had encountered Mr L.A., whose telephone he had used to call [the first applicant] ... Then Officer G.A. had arrived and ... several minutes later a Lada ‑ Priora car without registration numbers had also arrived with the head of the Novolak police station, Officer R. Kh., and two other officers, Z.M. and S.A. The officers had fired several gunshots in the air to ensure that Mr Danilin would not run away. After that the officers had put Timur Danilin in their car and taken him to the Khasavyurt Counterterrorism Centre. The residents of the houses situated in the vicinity had witnessed the incident. On the morning of 26 March 2012 the head of the Novolak police station had returned to the scene and warned the local residents to keep silent about the incident. To date, [the second applicant] has not been questioned about this incident; nor has Ms R., the mother of Officer G.A., been identified and questioned ... To verify the information concerning the persons detained at the Novolak police station between 25 and 27 March 2012, it is necessary ... to question all of the individuals who, according to the station’s detention log, were detained there and who could therefore verify whether Mr Danilin had been taken there ...”
28. On 4 April 2013 the investigators questioned the applicants about the complaint lodged by the second applicant with the investigators’ superiors. Their statements reaffirmed the information provided in the complaint (see the paragraph above).
29. Between April 2013 and March 2014 the investigation was suspended on several more occasions and each time it was resumed as a result of criticism by the investigators’ superiors, who stated that the suspensions had been premature and unlawful. On 20 April 2014 the investigation was suspended for the last time; the documents submitted show that the orders given by the superiors were not complied with.
30. It appears from the documents submitted that the investigation is still pending, the whereabouts of Mr Danilin have not been established and the perpetrators of his abduction have not been identified.
